title: 22. Interview: Apache Pulsar
summary: Interview Q&A for Apache Pulsar — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Apache Pulsar interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why does Pulsar separate brokers and bookies, and what does this buy operationally?
**Answer:** Pulsar's separation of stateless brokers (compute) from BookKeeper bookies (storage) means a broker holds no data on disk — it only owns a partition temporarily and writes entries to a quorum of bookies. The operational payoff appears during failure: when a broker dies, ZooKeeper detects it within seconds and reassigns its partitions to a surviving broker, which simply opens a new ledger on the same bookies. No data migration, no partition leader election, no waiting for in-sync replicas to catch up — historical ledgers stay exactly where they were. This makes broker failover near-instant (seconds, vs. Kafka's tens of seconds to minutes for partition leadership changes). A second benefit is independent scaling: if you need more write throughput you add brokers (compute), and if you need more retention you add bookies (storage) — neither forcing the other to scale. Tencent and Yahoo Japan rely on this property to run elastic, multi-tenant Pulsar clusters where individual teams' load spikes don't require rebalancing petabytes of historical data.
**Visual:**
```
Broker dies:                  Broker dies (Pulsar):
+----+ +----+ +----+          +----+ +----+ +----+
| B1 | | B2 | | B3 |          | B1 | | B2 | | B3 | (stateless)
+----+ +----+ +----+          +--X-+ +----+ +----+
  |     |     |                \     |     |
  v     v     v                 \    v     v
[data][data][data]               [bookies hold all data]
leader election, ISR wait        new broker opens new ledger
tens of seconds                  failover in seconds
```

### Q2. What are Pulsar's four subscription modes, and when would you pick each?
**Answer:** Pulsar supports four subscription modes on a single topic. **Exclusive** assigns the subscription to one consumer — appropriate when a single worker must process events in strict arrival order (e.g., a CDC stream feeding a database). **Shared** round-robins messages across N consumers with per-message ack — the workhorse for parallel processing of independent jobs like a notification fan-out, where any consumer can handle any message. **Failover** keeps one active consumer and N-1 hot standbys; on failure the next standby takes over in order — useful when you need ordered processing but also high availability, such as a single-writer session-state updater. **Key_Shared** is Pulsar's standout: messages with the same key always go to the same consumer, even across rebalances, so per-key ordering is preserved while overall throughput scales with consumer count. Use key_shared whenever you have per-entity ordering requirements (per-user event sequence, per-order state machine) but want horizontal parallelism — Kafka struggles to do this without losing per-key ordering during rebalances.
**Visual:**
```
Topic orders --> +------------------+------------------+------------------+
                 | exclusive (1)    | shared (N)       | key_shared (N)   |
                 | one consumer     | round-robin      | sticky by key    |
                 | strict order     | any msg -> any c | key -> same c    |
                 +------------------+------------------+------------------+
                 | failover (1+N)                        |
                 | active + standbys, ordered takeover   |
                 +---------------------------------------+
```

### Q3. How does Pulsar's geo-replication differ from Kafka's MirrorMaker 2?
**Answer:** Pulsar's geo-replication is built into the broker: a namespace is configured with a list of remote clusters (`us-east`, `eu-west`), and the broker automatically replicates produced messages to those clusters over dedicated internal links with their own backlog, retry, and rate-limit semantics. Producers write locally; consumers in each region read locally with low latency; cross-region lag is typically sub-second to seconds depending on network distance. There is no separate process to deploy, monitor, or restart. Kafka's MirrorMaker 2 (MM2), by contrast, is a separate cluster of consumer-producer bridges that consumes from the source Kafka and produces to the target Kafka. MM2 struggles with offset translation across clusters (consumer offsets don't map cleanly), requires careful configuration for exactly-once across the bridge, and is operationally another distributed system to run. Pulsar's native replication gives true active-active multi-region semantics with simpler operations, which is why Yahoo Japan and Tencent use it for cross-region active-active deployments where Kafka+MM2 would be operationally heavier.
**Visual:**
```
Pulsar:  prod -> Broker(us-east) --native repl--> Broker(eu-west) -> consumer
         (one system, one config)

Kafka:   prod -> Kafka(us-east) -> MM2 cluster -> Kafka(eu-west) -> consumer
         (three systems, offset translation pain)
```

### Q4. What is a BookKeeper ledger, and how does the quorum model work?
**Answer:** A ledger in BookKeeper is a write-once, append-only sequence of entries that is sealed (made immutable) when closed. Each partition in Pulsar is backed by a sequence of ledgers — when the current ledger fills, a new one is opened. Three parameters control replication: **ensemble size E** (how many bookies the ledger is spread across, typically 3), **write-quorum W** (how many bookies each entry is written to, typically 3), and **ack-quorum A** (how many must acknowledge before the broker acks the producer, typically 2). So with E=3, W=3, A=2, each entry is written to all 3 bookies and the producer gets an ack after 2 confirm — giving tolerance for 1 bookie failure without stalling writes. Reads can come from any bookie holding the entry. The ledger abstraction is also why broker failover is instant: a new broker simply opens a new ledger; the old ledgers remain readable on their original bookies and never need to be moved.
**Visual:**
```
entry e5 written:  E=3, W=3, A=2
bk1: [e5] ack ----+
bk2: [e5] ack ----+--> 2 acks received -> broker acks producer
bk3: [e5] ack ----   (3rd ack ignored, write succeeds even if bk3 slow)

Tolerates: 1 bookie down, write still acks via the other 2.
```

### Q5. How does tiered storage work in Pulsar, and when is it worth using?
**Answer:** Pulsar's tiered storage offloads sealed, aged ledgers from BookKeeper bookies to object storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS) while keeping them transparently readable through brokers. A namespace policy sets the threshold (e.g., offload ledgers older than 1 hour or larger than 100MB); once a ledger crosses the threshold, the broker coordinates upload of the ledger to object storage and BookKeeper releases local bookie capacity. Subsequent reads for that ledger are served from object storage — slower (tens of ms cold vs. ms warm) but at object-storage prices. The benefit is decoupling retention from bookie capacity: you can keep a year of telemetry for replay and compliance without provisioning petabytes of bookie SSD, paying cents-per-GB-month for cold data. The trade-off is latency for cold reads and bandwidth egress costs when consumers replay from old data. Use tiered storage when you have long-retention streaming topics (audit logs, raw event archives, ML training data) where recent data is hot and historical data is occasionally read — not for sub-second latency pipelines. Kafka added Tiered Storage (KIP-405) more recently and it is less mature.
**Visual:**
```
topic ledger timeline:
[L0 sealed][L1 sealed][L2 sealed][L3 active] <- recent
   |          |          |
   v          v          v   (age > 1h)
  S3         S3         S3   <-- cold, cheap
                          ^
   hot reads (ms) --------+------- cold reads (10s ms)
```

### Q6. What is the cursor in Pulsar, and how does it enable multiple independent subscriptions?
**Answer:** A cursor is a subscription's persistent position in a topic's log — the message ID of the last-acked (or last-delivered) message. Cursors are stored in ZooKeeper (or etcd in newer Pulsar versions) and updated as consumers ack, so a consumer restart resumes exactly where it left off. The key property is that **each subscription has its own independent cursor** on the same topic. This means one topic can serve many subscriptions with completely different consumption patterns: a `shared` billing subscription might be live (seconds behind), an `exclusive` CDC subscription might be hours behind replaying historical data, and a `key_shared` enrichment subscription might be paused and resumed on demand. The producer doesn't know or care about the subscribers; it just appends to the log. This is the same fan-out property Kafka provides via consumer groups, but Pulsar adds the flexibility of different subscription modes per consumer — so the same log can serve a queue-style consumer (shared) and a per-key-ordered consumer (key_shared) simultaneously.
**Visual:**
```
Topic log:   m0  m1  m2  m3  m4  m5  m6  m7  m8  m9
             ^                  ^           ^
cursor A:  [shared, acked to m9]              (live)
cursor B:  [exclusive, acked to m3]           (replaying)
cursor C:  [key_shared, acked to m7]          (live, per-key)
each cursor in ZooKeeper; producer unaware of any of them.
```

### Q7. What are Pulsar's main trade-offs vs. Kafka?
**Answer:** Pulsar's wins: instant broker failover (no leader election, no ISR stall) thanks to stateless brokers + BookKeeper; independent scaling of compute and storage; four subscription modes (exclusive, shared, failover, key_shared) vs. Kafka's one consumer-group model; native geo-replication built into the broker; mature tiered storage; and built-in multi-tenancy via `tenant/namespace/topic` URLs. Pulsar's losses: a smaller ecosystem (fewer connectors, fewer stream-processing libraries with first-class support, less community knowledge in the hiring market), higher operational complexity — you run two distributed systems (brokers + bookies) plus ZooKeeper — and historically slightly lower single-partition peak throughput than Kafka due to BookKeeper's quorum writes (each entry touches multiple bookies, vs. Kafka's single-leader write). The architect's rule: choose Pulsar when you need flexible subscription semantics, true multi-tenancy, geo-replication, or elastic independent scaling of storage and compute; choose Kafka for raw streaming throughput where the team already knows Kafka and the ecosystem matters; choose RabbitMQ for rich routing and per-message control at lower throughput.
**Visual:**
```
             Kafka             Pulsar            RabbitMQ
broker+storage  coupled         separated         broker-only
sub modes       1 (group)       4 (ex/sh/fo/ks)   exchanges
geo-repl        MM2 (separate)  native            federation
throughput      very high       high              medium
ecosystem       largest         medium            large
ops complexity  medium          higher (2 systems) low
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You run a multi-region payment platform and need each region's consumers to read locally with sub-second lag while maintaining global ordering per payment ID. How do you architect this on Pulsar?
**Answer:** Configure the `payments` namespace as a global namespace with replication to all regions (`us-east`, `us-west`, `eu-west`). Producers write to their local region's Pulsar cluster; the broker replicates each message to the remote clusters over native geo-replication links with sub-second to seconds cross-region lag. Consumers in each region attach a `key_shared` subscription keyed by `payment_id` to their local cluster — so the same payment's events always land on the same consumer within a region, preserving per-payment ordering, while overall throughput scales with consumer count. If a region fails, you fail over consumers to another region: their cursor (last-acked position) is recovered from ZooKeeper in that region, and they pick up from where they left off — there may be a small duplication window during failover, so consumers must be idempotent. Use producer-side dedup keys to avoid duplicates from producer retries. This pattern — global namespace + key_shared per region — is exactly how Tencent and Yahoo Japan run multi-region Pulsar for ordered, geo-distributed workloads.
**Visual:**
```
prod(us-east) -> Broker(us-east) --repl--> Broker(eu-west) -> key_shared cons
                   |                              |
                   v                              v
               key_shared cons (local, sub-ms)   key_shared cons (local)
               per-payment-id sticky             per-payment-id sticky
```

### Q2. A team needs to replay 30 days of historical events for a new ML feature without affecting live consumers or buying 30 days of bookie capacity. How do you do it on Pulsar?
**Answer:** Enable tiered storage on the topic's namespace with an offload threshold (e.g., offload ledgers older than 1 hour to S3). Live consumers read recent data from bookies at ms latency; the historical 30 days of ledgers live on S3 at object-storage cost (~$23/TB-month vs. ~10x for bookie SSD). When the new ML consumer subscribes with `SubscriptionType.Exclusive` and seeks to a 30-day-old message ID (using the `seek` API), the broker transparently fetches the relevant ledger entries from S3 — slower (tens of ms per batch cold) but functional — and replays them in order. The new subscription has its own cursor in ZooKeeper, so its replay does not disturb the live `shared` or `key_shared` subscriptions; they continue at full bookie speed. Configure the ML consumer with a reasonable prefetch and parallelism across partitions to amortize S3 latency. This pattern — tiered storage + seek-to-timestamp + independent cursor — lets you replay history at near-zero incremental infrastructure cost.
**Visual:**
```
topic ledger timeline (30 days):
[S3 old...][S3 old...][bookie recent]
                              ^ live consumers (ms)
   ^ ML consumer seeks here
   | cursor independent -> live consumers unaffected
```

### Q3. Your Pulsar cluster has a hot partition where one tenant's traffic is 10x others, causing that partition's broker to CPU-spike. How do you mitigate?
**Answer:** First, confirm via Pulsar's metrics (`pulsar_broker_producer_rate_per_topic`, per-partition backlog) which partition is hot and whether it's a single key concentrating traffic. Short-term mitigation: increase the topic's partition count (Pulsar supports dynamic partition expansion without breaking existing consumers — unlike Kafka, where adding partitions breaks key-based ordering), so the hot tenant's traffic spreads across more brokers. If the hot partition is caused by a single key (e.g., `user_id=42`), key_shared won't help — you need application-level sharding by splitting that key into N sub-keys (`user_42_0..user_42_N`) so traffic fans out. Medium-term: leverage Pulsar's built-in multi-tenancy to move the noisy tenant to a dedicated namespace with broker-side rate limiting (`dispatchRate`, `publishRate`), capping their impact on shared brokers. Long-term: add brokers (compute scales independently of storage) and let the load balancer redistribute partition ownership; BookKeeper absorbs the storage side without rebalancing data. The stateless-broker design means adding capacity is operationally simple.
**Visual:**
```
before: 1 partition = 1 broker (hot)
        +---P0---+ 10x rate -> broker CPU 100%
after:  split into 8 partitions
        +P0+P1+P2+P3+P4+P5+P6+P7+   (spread across 8 brokers)
        each ~1.25x rate -> CPU ~12% each
Pulsar: dynamic partition expand, consumers keep running.
```

### Q4. You migrated from Kafka and are seeing higher per-message write latency on Pulsar. What's likely the cause, and how do you tune it?
**Answer:** The likely cause is BookKeeper's quorum write — each entry is sent to W=3 bookies and acked after A=2, vs. Kafka's single-leader disk write. With default sync settings this can add a few ms of network round-trip per message. Tuning options: (1) **Batch aggressively** — set producer batching max messages (e.g., 1000) and max delay (e.g., 5ms) so the quorum overhead is amortized across many messages; Pulsar's batching can sustain millions of msgs/sec per broker. (2) **Lower ack-quorum** from A=2 to A=1 if your durability SLA permits (trades 1-bookie failure tolerance for lower latency). (3) **Use async producer** for non-critical writes — fire-and-forget with a callback collapses write latency to local queue time. (4) **Co-locate bookies** with brokers in the same rack/AZ to minimize network RTT. (5) **Tune BookKeeper journal flush** — by default BookKeeper fsyncs the journal per entry; if your durability SLA permits, batch journal flushes (e.g., `journalFlushDataWhenQueueIsFull` or group commit) to amortize fsync cost. The right combination typically closes the latency gap to Kafka while preserving Pulsar's separation benefits.
**Visual:**
```
Kafka:  prod -> leader broker -> fsync (1 disk write)         ~1-3ms
Pulsar: prod -> broker -> bk1 + bk2 + bk3, ack on 2           ~3-6ms (default)
        +batch 1000 msgs: amortize -> ~0.005ms/msg            (tuned)
        +ack_q=1: ~2ms                                         (lower durability)
```

### Q5. A consumer subscribed with `key_shared` is rebalancing, and you see brief per-key order violations during the rebalance. What's happening and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** Key_shared guarantees sticky per-key delivery during steady state, but during a rebalance — when a consumer joins or leaves — there is a transition window where a key's ownership may move from one consumer to another, and in-flight messages already delivered to the old consumer may not have been acked before the new consumer starts receiving the same key. Pulsar mitigates this with the `keySharedMode` setting: `AUTO_SPLIT` (default, may have brief overlap during rebalance) vs. `STICKY` (explicit hash-range assignment, more deterministic but slower to rebalance). To eliminate order violations: (1) Use `STICKY` mode with explicit key ranges if your key space is well-known. (2) Ensure consumers ack promptly — set a low `ackTimeoutMillis` and avoid long-running handlers that hold messages. (3) During planned scaling events, drain a consumer (pause its assignment) before removing it, so its in-flight messages are acked before ownership transfers. (4) If strict ordering is non-negotiable, fall back to `Failover` subscription for that key's stream — ordered but loses parallelism. The architect's rule: key_shared is best-effort per-key ordering with parallelism; if you need absolute ordering, accept failover's lower throughput.
**Visual:**
```
rebalance window:
   consumer A: key=user_42 (in-flight: m5,m6 unacked)
   ---------- ownership moves ----------
   consumer B: key=user_42 (receives m7, m8...)
   if m5,m6 ack after m7 received -> ORDER VIOLATION

fix: STICKY mode + drain on leave + prompt acks.
```

### Q6. You're designing a multi-tenant SaaS event bus where each tenant gets isolation but shares infrastructure. How does Pulsar help vs. Kafka?
**Answer:** Pulsar's URL structure `persistent://tenant/namespace/topic` makes multi-tenancy a first-class concept. Each tenant gets its own auth/ACL, quota (`publishRate`, `dispatchRate`, `backlogQuota`), retention policy, and geo-replication config at the namespace level — all enforced by the broker, no separate proxy needed. A noisy tenant's traffic is throttled at the namespace boundary and cannot starve other tenants. BookKeeper's storage is shared across tenants but isolated by namespace ledger ownership, and tiered storage can be enabled per-tenant. Kafka, by contrast, treats all topics uniformly — to get tenant isolation you deploy separate Kafka clusters per tenant (expensive, operational overhead) or run a proxy layer (Confluent's Multi-Tenant Geo-Replication, additional cost) to enforce quotas. The Pulsar model lets you run one cluster for 50 teams with per-tenant isolation enforced natively, while Kafka typically requires multiple clusters or third-party tooling. This is why Splunk and Tencent chose Pulsar for multi-tenant SaaS event buses.
**Visual:**
```
Pulsar cluster (1 cluster, 50 tenants):
  tenant A: prod/orders, prod/billing (own quota, ACL, retention)
  tenant B: prod/events               (own quota, ACL, retention)
  broker enforces per-namespace rate limits -> noisy tenant B
  cannot starve tenant A.

Kafka (typical multi-tenant SaaS):
  cluster A (tenant A) + cluster B (tenant B)  -> 2x ops cost
  OR single cluster + proxy layer              -> extra component
```

### Q7. A broker fails mid-write in your Pulsar cluster. Walk through what happens to in-flight and subsequent messages.
**Answer:** When a broker fails, ZooKeeper detects the loss of its ephemeral node within seconds (default heartbeat timeout ~30s, tunable). The broker owned certain partitions — say partition-0 of `orders` — and was mid-write of message `m5` to ledger `L17`. Three scenarios: (1) If `m5` was already acked to the producer (2 of 3 bookies confirmed), it's durable and will be readable by any new broker that opens ledger L17 for reads. (2) If `m5` was in flight (sent to bookies but not yet acked), the producer's send will time out and the producer retries to whichever broker now owns partition-0 — Pulsar producers auto-detect broker ownership changes via ZooKeeper lookups, so the retry lands on the new broker, which writes `m5` to a new ledger. (3) Subsequent messages from producers route to the new broker after they refresh ownership metadata. Because bookies hold all data and ledgers are immutable once sealed, no data migration is needed — the new broker opens a fresh ledger and continues. Consumers see a brief pause (seconds) during ownership transfer, then resume from their cursor in ZooKeeper. This is the operational payoff of Pulsar's separation: failures are fast and data-safe.
**Visual:**
```
T0: B1 owns p0, writes m5 to L17 (bk1, bk2, bk3)
T1: B1 dies -> ZK detects (~30s)
T2: B2 takes ownership of p0, opens new ledger L18
T3: producer retries m5 (unacked) -> B2 writes m5 to L18
T4: consumers resume from cursor (in ZK) reading L17 + L18
no data migration, no leader election, no ISR wait.
```
